idiom_name: shared references (&T) for queries, ownership and &mut for commands; const fn for compile time
implementation_notes: Rust encodes the query/command split in the type system: a function taking &T cannot mutate what it borrows (only interior mutability can, and it shows in the type), while a function that changes state must take &mut T or ownership, which excludes aliases for the duration of the call. The Rust Book states the rule as mutable and immutable borrows being mutually exclusive, and the Reference notes that a shared reference prevents direct mutation of the value. Value types with Clone/Copy and owned return values make copy-on-update ordinary, so the classic defensive-copy discipline is replaced by the borrow checker; reach for Cell/RefCell/Mutex only at edges that genuinely need shared mutation, and use const fn when the computation must also be usable at compile time.
pitfalls: Interior mutability reintroduces effects behind a shared reference: RefCell panics on a conflicting borrow at runtime, and a Mutex can deadlock or poison.
The signature does not stop I/O or ambient reads - println!, std::fs and SystemTime::now look exactly like a pure function to the borrow checker.
const fn is a restricted subset (no heap allocation, limited control flow in older editions), so not every pure computation can be constant-evaluated.
